newsitem.title: DENMARK: Analysts welcome Danish 1997 state budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Analysts welcome Danish 1997 state budget deal.

text.p: Danish analysts contacted by Reuters on Thursday broadly welcomed the minority government's pact with the far-left opposition, which appeared to guarantee passage of its 1997 budget and ensure its survival for the immediate future.

"It is not a terribly impressive deal but it does seem to guarantee some measure of political calm in the new year," said director Mads Jacobsen at Den Danske Bank, the country's biggest banking institution.
"The budget is not going to trigger premature elections and that is positive news," he added.

On Wednesday night the Social Democrat-led coalition won the agreement of the Socialist Peoples' Party (SPP) to a deal balancing the public sector budget by liquidating a maritime war damage fund and a state property agency and transferring money from a workers' holiday fund.
Economist Jesper Nielsen at Unidanmark, Denmark's second largest bank, was less enthusiastic.
"It seems rather cosmetic to balance the public sector budget by lifting money from the war damage fund even if the whole thing looks all right on paper," Nielsen said.
"It could have been much worse. The Socialist Peoples' Party has showed more responsibility than at any other point in the past decade," he added.
The Danish stock and bond markets were largely unmoved by the budget deal, though some bond dealers had expected a negative reaction from overseas investors.
"The government does not seem to have been forced to make any major concessions to win SPP support for its budget," one dealer told Reuters.
The SPP agreed to support the budget in parliament in return for increased funding for education, social projects and improved health and safety at work measures.
The 1997 state budget has to be passed by parliament before it goes on Christmas recess on December 19. --Chris Follett, Copenhagen newsroom +45-33969652
